props.title: The Rules of Attraction
props.initialSlug: Sex, drugs, and darkness at elite college

sections.content: The Rules of Attraction marked a pivotal moment in dark campus cinema, with Roger Avary adapting Bret Easton Ellis's nihilistic novel into a frenetic exploration of privileged college life. The film's innovative techniques - including split-screens, reversed footage, and a legendary 5-minute Europe sequence shot in fast motion - influenced countless indie films that followed. Like its literary counterpart, it serves as a companion piece to American Psycho (2000), sharing the character of Patrick Bateman through his younger brother Sean, played with calculated emptiness by James Van Der Beek.

sections.content: The film's portrayal of campus hedonism connects to earlier works like Animal House (1978), but strips away the comedy to expose raw desperation. Director Avary, fresh from co-writing Pulp Fiction (1994), brings a nonlinear storytelling approach that emphasizes the characters' disconnection. The infamous suicide scene, shown from multiple perspectives, demonstrates how the film uses technical innovation to underscore emotional emptiness.

What sets The Rules of Attraction apart is its unflinching look at privilege and nihilism in higher education, themes later explored in films like The Social Network (2010) and Thoroughbreds (2017). The film's influence can be seen in the cynical campus narratives of Dear White People (2014) and the dark sexuality of Spring Breakers (2012). SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Cinema

sections.content: The film's technical innovations have become increasingly relevant in the social media age. Its split-screen sequences and rapid-cut montages predicted the fractured attention spans of modern viewers. The Europe sequence, showing Victor's debauched vacation, created a template for fast-cut travel montages that became ubiquitous in films like The Secret Life of Walter Mitty (2013) and Garden State (2004).
